problem-solution.name: Problem → Solution
problem-solution.summary: Classic business arc: name the pain, raise the stakes, present your fix, show how it works, prove it, ask. The default for sales decks, internal proposals, and most general business presentations.

beats.name: Hook
beats.description: Open with a striking question, statistic, customer quote, or moment that earns the audience's attention. The goal is to make them want to hear what comes next, not to convey information.

beats.name: The Problem
beats.description: Name the pain in concrete terms. Make it visceral and specific — describe who hurts, how, and what they're trying to do today that isn't working. Avoid abstractions; use real examples or scenarios the audience recognizes.

beats.name: Why It Matters
beats.description: Quantify the cost of inaction or the upside of action. Use numbers, trends, customer impact, competitive pressure — whatever makes the audience feel the size of the problem and care about solving it now rather than later.

beats.name: The Solution
beats.description: Reveal your approach and what it produces for the customer. Lead with the outcome, not the architecture. Keep it concrete: what does the audience get, and what changes for them?

beats.name: How It Works
beats.description: Show the moving parts that make the solution credible. Walk through the key mechanism, workflow, or technical insight that explains why this approach succeeds where others have failed. Enough detail to earn trust; not so much that you lose the room.

beats.name: Proof
beats.description: Demonstrate the solution works. Use customer logos, before/after metrics, demos, case studies, third-party validation — whatever de-risks the claim. One strong piece of proof beats three weak ones.

beats.name: The Ask
beats.description: State a clear, specific call to action. What do you want the audience to do, decide, or commit to next? Make the smallest credible ask that moves things forward, and make it unambiguous.

investor.name: Investor
investor.summary: Angel investors, VCs, or institutional investors evaluating financial viability, market opportunity, and team.
investor.description: Angel, venture, and institutional investors judging financial viability, market opportunity, and the team. Lead with traction, size the market (TAM, SAM, SOM), make the moat and differentiation explicit, and show financial projections with their assumptions stated. Moderate chart density; 12-20 slides.

regulatory.name: Regulatory / Compliance
regulatory.summary: Government agencies, auditors, or compliance bodies reviewing adherence to rules and standards.
regulatory.description: Government agencies, auditors, and compliance bodies reviewing adherence to rules and standards. Lead with evidence, date-stamp material, cite document references, and map each claim to the requirement it satisfies. Moderate chart density; 20-40 slides with an appendix.

report.name: Report
report.summary: Summarize performance, progress, or findings with enough context to interpret results.
report.description: Use for business reviews, project updates, research summaries, and recurring operating cadences. Prioritize the metric, the movement, the reason, and the implication.
report.outcome: The audience understands what happened, why it happened, and what it means.
successCriteria: Key metrics are easy to scan

inspirational.name: Inspirational
inspirational.summary: Aspirational, narrative-driven voice for keynotes, founders, and rallying cries.
inspirational.description: Reach for shared belief and possibility, then ground it in something concrete. Use vivid imagery and rhythm; avoid collapsing into hype by always pairing aspiration with a real anchor.
voiceCues: Open with belief; close with action.
Use rhythm — paired phrases, repetition, deliberate beats.
Pair every aspirational claim with a concrete proof point.
Speak in present tense to make the future feel inevitable.
avoid: Stacked superlatives ('the very best, world-changing, revolutionary').
Dense data tables — push numbers into supporting slides.
samplePhrases: We're building the runtime that makes agents feel instant.
When latency disappears, what becomes possible?
The next decade of software belongs to teams who treat speed as a feature.

classic.name: Classic
classic.description: A timeless, clean, and versatile theme with balanced color contrasts and classic typography. Ideal for professional, readable presentations.

slate-gray.name: Slate Gray
slate-gray.summary: Neutral gray palette for understated executive communication.
slate-gray.description: A disciplined gray scale with strong neutral contrast. Use it when the content should feel calm, mature, and analytical.

cool-horizon.name: Cool Horizon
cool-horizon.summary: Cool blue-green palette tuned for professional business decks.
cool-horizon.description: A balanced cool-toned scheme with deep navy, business blues, and teal accents. It works well across strategy, finance, and technical narratives.

tenorite.name: Tenorite
tenorite.description: Tenorite is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Tenorite Display for headings with Tenorite for body text.

cover.name: Cover
cover.summary: The opening slide: title, subtitle and an optional picture.
cover.description: Open a presentation with its subject and a short introduction. Add a picture when it helps establish the context.

text.name: Text
text.summary: Prose. Several blocks sit side by side when short and stack when long.
text.description: Explain one idea in continuous prose. Use paragraphs or flowing blocks for detail that needs to be read in sequence.

chart.name: Chart
chart.summary: One to six charts, with an optional note.
chart.description: Give a chart enough space to show its evidence. Use the title to state the conclusion and labels to explain the measures.

table-beside.name: Table beside
table-beside.summary: A table with commentary beside it.
table-beside.description: Place a table beside its interpretation. Use the supporting text to explain the conclusion without repeating every cell.

timeline.name: Timeline
timeline.summary: Dated events or a roadmap along one axis, with optional notes.
timeline.description: Show events or milestones in chronological order. Label each item with a date or stage and a concise description.

list.name: List
list.summary: Bulleted or numbered points; one long list flows into columns.
list.description: Present several related points in a clear sequence. Use bullets for independent points or numbered items for an ordered list.
